clinicalPearls: Typically affects men over 50 and presents with lower urinary tract symptoms that are grouped into voiding (hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, straining, incomplete emptying) and storage (frequency, urgency, nocturia) categories
Symptom severity correlates poorly with prostate size, so a large gland may be asymptomatic while a small gland can cause significant obstruction
Digital rectal examination usually reveals a smooth, firm, symmetrically enlarged gland; nodularity, asymmetry, or a hard area should raise suspicion of malignancy
The International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) is useful for quantifying symptom burden and monitoring response to treatment
Medical management principles include alpha-blockers to relax prostatic smooth muscle for rapid symptom relief and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors to shrink the gland over months in larger prostates
Absolute surgical indications include refractory retention, recurrent urinary infection, bladder stones, recurrent haematuria, and upper tract dilatation or renal impairment from obstruction
Transurethral resection of the prostate remains the reference surgical standard, with newer minimally invasive and laser techniques offering alternatives
PSA may be mildly elevated due to gland volume, but a significantly raised or rising level warrants evaluation for prostate cancer
reference.pathophysiology: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is a proliferation of glandular epithelial and stromal cells in the transition zone of the prostate, driven by ageing and androgen (dihydrotestosterone) activity. The enlarging gland produces a static component of obstruction by mechanical narrowing of the prostatic urethra and a dynamic component from increased smooth muscle tone mediated by alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. Chronic outflow obstruction leads to detrusor muscle hypertrophy, trabeculation, and eventually detrusor decompensation, incomplete emptying, and rising post-void residual volumes, with risk of upper tract dilatation and renal impairment in advanced cases.
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis to exclude infection and haematuria
Serum creatinine and renal function assessment
PSA measurement with counselling about interpretation
Post-void residual volume by bladder ultrasound
Uroflowmetry to assess flow rate and obstructive pattern
Renal and bladder ultrasound to assess upper tracts, bladder wall, and residual urine
Pressure-flow urodynamics in equivocal or complex cases
redFlags: Acute urinary retention, a urological emergency requiring prompt catheterisation
Obstructive uropathy with hydronephrosis and renal impairment
Recurrent urinary infection or urosepsis associated with an obstructed, incompletely emptying bladder
Gross or persistent haematuria requiring exclusion of malignancy
Hard, nodular, or asymmetric prostate on examination suggesting cancer
reference.prognosis: BPH is a slowly progressive condition; many men remain stable or improve with medical therapy, but a subset progress to retention or complications requiring surgery, which generally produces durable symptom relief.
pitfalls: Attributing all lower urinary tract symptoms to the prostate and missing bladder dysfunction, cancer, or stricture
Overlooking chronic high-residual retention presenting with overflow incontinence and silent renal impairment
Relying on prostate size alone to judge the need for treatment
Failing to counsel that 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors lower PSA and take months to act
Missing prostate cancer masked by a benign clinical picture
management: Offer watchful waiting with lifestyle and fluid advice for mild lower urinary tract symptoms with low symptom burden
Start an alpha-blocker to relax prostatic smooth muscle for rapid relief of the dynamic component of obstruction
Add a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor to shrink larger glands over months and reduce progression, using combination therapy where appropriate
Consider an antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist for predominant storage symptoms, and a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor where erectile dysfunction coexists
Monitor with the International Prostate Symptom Score and surveillance of renal function and post-void residual volume

Refer for surgery such as transurethral resection of the prostate for refractory symptoms or absolute indications including refractory retention, recurrent infection, bladder stones, recurrent haematuria or upper tract dilatation
Manage acute urinary retention with catheterisation followed by a trial without catheter under alpha-blocker cover
